title: 7.7 Small Group · Group 2

languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

noticeAndWonder.context: Detective Chen is comparing two case notes. Note A says: 'The evidence locker holds exactly 54 files, split equally among 6 shelves.' Note B says: 'The surveillance van must stay parked for no more than 45 minutes.' Look closely at the phrases 'split equally... exactly' in Note A versus 'no more than' in Note B. What do you notice about how the wording is different, and what do you wonder about which situations need an equation with an equal sign versus an inequality?
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Overtime Hours Limit
revealWordProblem.text: Detective Chen's team can use at most 40 hours of overtime this week to close the case. So far the team has logged 26 hours. Write an inequality for the additional overtime hours t the team can still use, solve it, and graph the solution set on a number line.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The inequality is 26 + t ≤ 40. Subtracting 26 from both sides: t ≤ 40 − 26 = 14. Since ≤ includes the boundary, graph a closed circle at 14 and shade left (toward smaller values), meaning the team can use 14 or fewer additional overtime hours this week.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — Should I model this problem with an equation or an inequality?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 'Equals' or 'exactly' points to an equation (=); 'at least, at most, more than, fewer than' points to an inequality — and you can explain why it works, even when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Clue: 'A total divided equally among 4 people gave each $85.'
This has an exact total, so I use an equation. Let t be the total.
Divided among 4 to get 85 means t ÷ 4 = 85, so t = 85 × 4 = 340.
Check reasonableness: $340 split 4 ways is $85 each. That makes sense!

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Read each word problem. Decide if it needs an equation or an inequality. Write the mathematical model, solve it, and check your answer for reasonableness. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

rows.wordProblem: A detective splits 42 clues equally among 6 case boards. How many clues per board?
rows.reasonable: Yes — 7 clues per board makes sense.

rows.wordProblem: A witness says the suspect carried fewer than 10 items. If the suspect already had 3, how many more could they carry?
rows.reasonable: Yes — up to 6 more items is reasonable.

rows.wordProblem: The evidence room needs at least 50 storage bins. They already have 28. How many more do they need?
rows.reasonable: Yes — at least 22 more bins makes sense.

hints: If the problem uses 'is,' 'equals,' or 'gives exactly,' use an equation (=). If it uses 'at least,' 'at most,' 'more than,' or 'fewer than,' use an inequality.
After solving, ask: Does my answer make sense in the real-world context? Could the number be negative? A fraction of a person?
explore.label: For each word problem, write the model, solve, and check for reasonableness.

discourse.prompt: How do you decide whether a word problem needs an equation or an inequality?
discourse.sentenceFrame: I use an equation when the problem says ___, but I use an inequality when the problem says ___ because ___.

onLevel.stem: A student solved 4n = 52 and got n = 13. Is the answer reasonable if n represents the number of notebooks in a box?
choices: Yes — 13 notebooks per box is reasonable
Yes — but only if n is a fraction
onLevel.explanation: 4 × 13 = 52 ✓. 13 notebooks per box is a reasonable whole number answer.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: 'Reasonable' asks two things: does the math check out, AND does the number make sense for notebooks in a box?
Check the math first: multiply 4 by 13 and see if it rebuilds 52. Then judge whether that count fits a real box of notebooks.
Compute 4 × 13. Does it equal 52? Then ask: could a box realistically hold that many notebooks? Match your reasoning to one choice.

onLevel.title: onLevel — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Seven evidence lockers hold 84 case files in all, split equally. How many files per locker?

onLevel.correctWork: The variable f is multiplied by 7, so you undo it by dividing both sides by 7 (the inverse operation), not by subtracting 7. 7f = 84 becomes f = 84 ÷ 7 = 12. So there are 12 files per locker. Check: 7 × 12 = 84 ✓
hints: f is multiplied by 7. What operation undoes multiplying by 7 — subtracting 7 or dividing by 7?
Divide both sides by 7: f = 84 ÷ 7 = 12 files per locker.

onLevel.title: Find the Problem-Solving Error

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: A parking lot holds at most 200 cars. There are 134 already. How many more can park?

onLevel.correctWork: 'At most' means less than or equal to, so the model should be an inequality: 134 + c ≤ 200. Solving: c ≤ 66. Up to 66 more cars can park, not exactly 66.
hints: The problem says 'at most 200.' Does that mean exactly 200 or up to 200?
'At most' requires ≤, not =. The correct model is 134 + c ≤ 200, so c ≤ 66.

extending.stem: Room 2: The vault keypad clue reads, 'A number of stolen coins plus 6 equals 14.' Solve x + 6 = 14 to find the code x.
extending.explanation: Subtract 6 from both sides: x = 14 − 6 = 8. Check: 8 + 6 = 14 ✓
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.

extending.stem: Room 3: A sign warns, 'The safe holds at most 20 gold bars.' Which inequality models the number of bars x?
extending.explanation: 'At most 20' means 20 or fewer, so x ≤ 20.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.

extending.stem: Room 4: A locked drawer clue reads, 'Five identical evidence boxes weigh 60 pounds in all.' Solve 5w = 60 for each box's weight w.
extending.explanation: Divide both sides by 5: w = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 pounds. Check: 5 × 12 = 60 ✓
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.

extending.title: Level 2 Extension — The Final Door: Catch the Detective's Mistake

workedExample.label: Clue
workedExample.work: Solve the keypad inequality 3x ≤ 18 to find how many bars x fit.

workedExample.label: Step 2
workedExample.work: Divide only the left side by 3: 3x ÷ 3 ≤ 18

extending.correctWork: Whatever you do to one side of an inequality, you must do to the OTHER side too. Dividing only the left side by 3 breaks the balance. 3x ≤ 18 becomes 3x ÷ 3 ≤ 18 ÷ 3, which gives x ≤ 6. So at most 6 bars fit, not 18.
hints: The left side was divided by 3, but was the right side divided by 3 too?
Divide BOTH sides by 3: 3x ÷ 3 ≤ 18 ÷ 3, so x ≤ 6.

extending.stem: A museum has some paintings. After adding 12, they have 45. Which equation models this?
extending.explanation: 'Adding 12' to the original number gives 45: p + 12 = 45. Solve: p = 33.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: The museum STARTS with an unknown number of paintings p, then 12 more are ADDED to reach 45.
'Adding 12' means the model joins p and 12 with a plus sign, and the total 45 goes after the equals sign.
Write the story in order: p, plus 12, equals 45. Which choice matches without switching the operation?

extending.stem: A detective needs more than 8 hours to finish the investigation. She has already worked 3 hours. Which inequality represents the additional hours h she needs?
extending.explanation: 3 hours plus additional hours h must be more than 8: 3 + h > 8. Solve: h > 5.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: There are two time pieces: the 3 hours already worked and the extra hours h. Together they must pass 8 hours.
'More than 8' means the TOTAL of 3 + h sits on the big side of a strict inequality — not an equals sign.
Combine first: 3 + h. Then compare that total to 8 using the strict 'more than' symbol. Which choice is built that way?

extending.stem: Which model is correct for: 'A number divided by 6 equals 7'?
extending.explanation: Divided by 6 is n / 6. Equals 7 means = 7. So n / 6 = 7.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: Spot the operation phrase: 'divided by 6'. That phrase gives you the symbol between n and 6.
Keep the sentence order — the number n comes first, then the division by 6, then 'equals 7'.
Write n / 6 on the left and 7 on the right. Which choice shows division rather than multiplying or adding 6?

extending.stem: A bus can carry at most 48 passengers. There are already 31 on board. Which inequality shows how many more can board?
extending.explanation: 'At most 48' means the total must be ≤ 48. So 31 + p ≤ 48. Solve: p ≤ 17.
choiceFeedback: Check your operation. Re-read what the problem asks.
hints: The bus already has 31 riders, and p more may board — but the TOTAL cannot pass 48.
'At most 48' allows exactly 48 but nothing above it, so you need the symbol with the 'or equal' bar, not > or =.
Add the parts first: 31 + p. Then cap that sum at 48 with the 'at most' symbol. Which choice matches?

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Equations and Inequalities Problem Solving is matching the wrong model to a key phrase. For 'the getaway car held no more than 6 bags,' students often write the equation b = 6 instead of the inequality b ≤ 6, because they see one number and assume it must be exact. The same mistake happens in reverse: for 'the reward split equally among 5 people gave each $40,' students sometimes write the inequality 5p ≥ 40 instead of the equation 5p = 40, because 'split equally' sounds like it could mean a range. Before you submit, ask: does this phrase give one exact value (equation, =) or a limit/range (inequality, <, >, ≤, ≥)?

connect.scenario: A detective has a $500 budget for equipment. She has already spent $320. The inequality 320 + r ≤ 500 represents the remaining amount r she can spend. She also needs exactly 4 flashlights at $15 each, represented by the equation 4f = 60.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — A box of donuts has some donuts. After giving away 7, there are fewer than 5 left. Which inequality represents the starting number of donuts d?
exitTicket.explanation: Starting with d donuts and giving away 7 leaves fewer than 5: d − 7 < 5. Solve: d < 12. ✓
choiceFeedback: She gave donuts away, so subtract 7, don't add it.
'Fewer than 5' means less than 5 — use '<', not '>'.
'Fewer than' is an inequality, not equal — use '<'.
hints: Track the story: start with d donuts, GIVE AWAY 7, and what remains is FEWER than 5.
'Giving away' means subtracting from d, and 'fewer than 5' means the strict less-than symbol — not equals and not greater-than.
Build it in story order: d, minus 7, then compare what's left to 5 using '<'. Which choice matches that structure?
